entries.f5d19b908efed58d55d6ee3db8af2d999ab83e42: <div sID="gen32621" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Titus.2" sID="Titus.2"/> <div eID="gen32621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32622" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32623" type="x-p"/> The apostle here directs Titus about the faithful discharge of his own office generally (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.1">ver. 1</reference>), and particularly as to several sorts of persons (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.2-Titus.2.10">ver. 2-10</reference>) and gives the grounds of these and of other following directions (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.11-Titus.2.14">ver. 11-14</reference>), with a summary direction in the close, <reference osisRef="Titus.2.15">ver. 15</reference>.
entries.a2bc2f222e92e95cd5ecb0907eaea4b65dd14e06: <div eID="gen32623" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32622" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Relative Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32624" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> But speak thou the things which become sound doctrine: <hi type="super">2</hi> That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience. <hi type="super">3</hi> The aged women likewise, that <hi type="italic">they be</hi> in behaviour as becometh holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things; <hi type="super">4</hi> That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, <hi type="super">5</hi> <hi type="italic">To be</hi> discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed. <hi type="super">6</hi> Young men likewise exhort to be sober minded. <hi type="super">7</hi> In all things showing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine <hi type="italic">showing</hi> uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity, <hi type="super">8</hi> Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you. 9 <hi type="italic">Exhort</hi> servants to be obedient unto their own masters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to please <hi type="italic">them</hi> well in all <hi type="italic">things;</hi> not answering again; <hi type="super">10</hi> Not purloining, but showing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things. <div eID="gen32624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32625" type="x-p"/> Here is the third thing in the matter of the epistle. In the chapter foregoing, the apostle had directed Titus about matters of government, and to set in order the things that were wanting in the churches. Now here he exhorts him, <div eID="gen32625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32626" type="x-p"/> I. Generally, to a faithful discharge of his own office. His ordaining others to preach would not excuse himself from preaching, nor might he take care of ministers and elders only, but he must instruct private Christians also in their duty. The adversative particle (<hi type="italic">but</hi>) here points back to the corrupt teachers, who vented <hi type="italic">fables,</hi> things vain and unprofitable: in opposition to them, says he, "<hi type="italic">But speak thou the things that become sound doctrine,</hi> what is agreeable to the word, which is pure and uncorrupt, healthful and nourishing to eternal life." Observe, (1.) The true doctrines of the gospel are <hi type="italic">sound doctrines,</hi> formally and effectively; they are in themselves good and holy, and make the believers so; they make them fit for, and vigorous in, the service of God. (2.) Ministers must be careful to teach only such truths. If the common talk of Christians must <hi type="italic">be uncorrupt, to the use of edifying, such as may minister grace to the hearers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.29">Eph. iv. 29</reference>), much more must ministers' preaching be such. Thus the apostle exhorts Titus generally: and then, <div eID="gen32626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32627" type="x-p"/> II. Specially and particularly, he instructs him to apply this sound doctrine to several sorts of persons, from <reference osisRef="Titus.2.2-Titus.2.10">v. 2-10</reference>. Ministers must not stay in generals, but must divide to every one his portion, what belongs to his age, or place, or condition of life; they must be particular as well as practical in their preaching; they must teach men their duty, and must teach all and each his duty. Here is an excellent Christian directory, accommodated to the old and to the young; to men and women; to the preacher himself and to servants. <div eID="gen32627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32628" type="x-p"/> 1. To the aged men. By aged men some understand elders by office, including deacons, &c. But it is rather to be taken of the aged in point of years. Old disciples of Christ must conduct themselves in every thing agreeably to the Christian doctrine. <hi type="italic">That the aged men be sober,</hi> not thinking that the decays of nature, which they feel in old age, will justify them in any inordinacy or intemperance, whereby they conceit to repair them; they must keep measure in things, both for health and for fitness, for counsel and example to the younger. <hi type="italic">Grave:</hi> levity is unbecoming in any, but especially in the aged; they should be composed and stayed, grave in habit, speech, and behaviour; gaudiness in dress, levity and vanity in the behaviour, how unbeseeming in their years! <hi type="italic">Temperate,</hi> moderate and prudent, one who governs well his passions and affections, so as not to be hurried away by them to any thing that is evil or indecent. <hi type="italic">Sound in the faith,</hi> sincere and stedfast, constantly adhering to the truth of the gospel, not fond of novelties, nor ready to run into corrupt opinions or parties, nor to be taken with Jewish fables or traditions, or the dotages of their rabbin. Those who are full of years should be full of grace and goodness, the inner man renewing more and more as the outer decays. <hi type="italic">In charity,</hi> or love; this is fitly joined with <hi type="italic">faith,</hi> which works by, and must be seen in, love, love to God and men, and soundness therein. It must be sincere love, without dissimulation: love of God for himself, and of men for God's sake. The duties of the second table must be done in virtue of those of the first; love to men as men, and to the saints as the excellent of the earth, in whom must be special delight; and love at all times, in adversity as well as prosperity. Thus must there be soundness in charity or love. And <hi type="italic">in patience.</hi> Aged persons are apt to be peevish, fretful, and passionate; and therefore need to be on their guard against such infirmities and temptations. Faith, love, and patience, are three main Christian graces, and soundness in these is much of gospel perfection. There is <hi type="italic">enduring patience</hi> and <hi type="italic">waiting patience,</hi> both of which must be looked after; to <hi type="italic">bear evils</hi> becomingly, and contentedly to <hi type="italic">want the good</hi> till we are fit for it and it for us, being <hi type="italic">followers of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.</hi> Thus as to the aged men. <div eID="gen32628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32629" type="x-p"/> 2. To the aged women. These also must be instructed and warned. Some by these aged women understand the deaconesses, who were mostly employed in looking after the poor and attending the sick; but it is rather to be taken (as we render it) of all aged women professing religion. They must <hi type="italic">be in behaviour as becometh holiness:</hi> both men and women must accommodate their behaviour to their profession. Those virtues before mentioned (<hi type="italic">sobriety, gravity, temperance, soundness in the faith, charity, and patience</hi>), recommended to aged men, are not proper to them only, but applicable to both sexes, and to be looked to by aged women as well as men. Women are to hear and learn their duty from the word, as well as the men: there is not one way of salvation for one sex or sort, and another for another; but both must learn and practise the same things, both as aged and as Christians; the virtues and duties are common. <hi type="italic">That the aged women likewise</hi> (as well as the men) <hi type="italic">be in behaviour as becometh holiness;</hi> or as beseems and is proper for holy persons, such as they profess to be and should be, keeping a pious decency and decorum in clothing and gesture, in looks and speech, and all their deportment, and this from an inward principle and habit of holiness, influencing and ordering the outward conduct at all times. Observe, Though express scripture do not occur, or be not brought, for every word, or look, or fashion in particular, yet general rules there are according to which all must be ordered; as <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1 Cor. x. 31</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.</hi> And <reference osisRef="Phil.4.8">Phil. iv. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure, whatsoever things are lovely, whatsoever things are of good report, if there be any virtue, and if there be any praise, think on these things.</hi> And here, whatsoever things are beseeming or unbeseeming holiness form a measure and rule of conduct to be looked to. <hi type="italic">Not false accusers</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">me diabolous,</hi></hi> no calumniators or sowers of discord, slandering and backbiting their neighbours, a great and too common fault; not only loving to speak, but to speak ill, of people, and to separate very friends. A slanderer is one <hi type="italic">whose tongue is set on fire of hell;</hi> so much, and so directly, do these do the devil's work, that for it the devil's name is given to such. This is a sin contrary to the great duties of love, justice, and equity between one another; it springs often from malice and hatred, or envy, and such like evil causes, to be shunned as well as the effect. <hi type="italic">Not given to much wine;</hi> the word denotes such addictedness thereto as to be under the power and mastery of it. This is unseemly and evil in any, but especially in this sex and age, and was too much to be found among the Greeks of that time and place. How immodest and shameful, corrupting and destroying purity both of body and mind! Of what evil example and tendency, unfitting for the thing, which is a positive duty of aged matrons, namely, to be <hi type="italic">teachers of good things!</hi> Not public preachers, that is forbidden (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1 Cor. xiv. 34</reference>, <hi type="italic">I permit not a woman to speak in the church</hi>), but otherwise teach they may and should, that is, by example and good life. Hence observe, Those whose actions and behaviour become holiness are thereby teachers of good things; and, besides this, they may and should also teach by doctrinal instruction at home, and in a private way. <hi type="italic">The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy his mother taught him.</hi> Such a woman is praised, <hi type="italic">She openeth her mouth with wisdom, and in her tongue is the law of kindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.31.1">Prov. xxxi. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.26">26</reference>. <hi type="italic">Teachers of good things</hi> are opposed to teachers of things corrupt, or to what is trifling and vain, of no good use or tendency, old wives' fables or superstitious sayings and observances; in opposition to these, their business is, and they may be called on to it, to be teachers of good things. <div eID="gen32629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32630" type="x-p"/> 3. There are lessons for young women also, whom the aged women must teach, instructing and advising them in the duties of religion according to their years. For teaching such things aged women have often better access than the men, even than ministers have, which therefore they must improve in instructing the young women, especially the young wives; for he speaks of their duty to their husbands and children. These young women the more aged must teach, (1.) To bear a good personal character: <hi type="italic">To be sober and discreet,</hi> contrary to the vanity and rashness which younger years are subject to: discreet in their judgments and sober in their affections and behaviour. <hi type="italic">Discreet</hi> and <hi type="italic">chaste</hi> stand well together; many expose themselves to fatal temptations by that which at first might be but indiscretion. <reference osisRef="Prov.2.11">Prov. ii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Discretion shall preserve thee, understanding shall keep thee from the evil way. Chaste,</hi> and <hi type="italic">keepers at home,</hi> are well joined too. Dinah, when she went to see the daughters of the land, lost her chastity. Those whose home is their prison, it is to be feared, feel that their chastity is their fetters. Not but there are occasions, and will be, of going abroad; but a gadding temper for merriment and company sake, to the neglect of domestic affairs, or from uneasiness at being in her place, is the opposite evil intended, which is commonly accompanied with, or draws after it, other evils. <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13-1Tim.5.14">1 Tim. v. 13, 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">They learn to be idle, wandering from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.</hi> Their business is <hi type="italic">to guide the house,</hi> and they should give no occasion to the enemy to speak reproachfully. <hi type="italic">Good,</hi> generally, in opposition to all vice; and specially, in her place, kind, helpful, and charitable; as Dorcas, <hi type="italic">full of good works and almsdeeds.</hi> It may also have, as some think, a more particular sense; one of a meek and yet cheerful spirit and temper, not sullen nor bitter; not taunting not fretting and galling any; not of a troublesome or jarring disposition, uneasy in herself and to those about her; but of a good nature and pleasing conversation, and likewise helpful by her advice and pains: thus <hi type="italic">building her house, and doing her husband good, and not evil, all her days.</hi> Thus in their personal character <hi type="italic">sober, discreet, chaste, keepers at home,</hi> and <hi type="italic">good:</hi> and, (2.) In their relative capacities: <hi type="italic">To love their husbands, and to be obedient to them;</hi> and where there is true love this will be no difficult command. God, in nature, and by his will, hath made this subordination: <hi type="italic">I suffer not a woman to usurp authority over the man</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.12">1 Tim. ii. 12</reference>); and the reason is added: <hi type="italic">For Adam was first formed, then Eve. Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being deceived, was in the transgression,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13-Titus.2.14">v. 13, 14</reference>. She fell first, and was the means of seducing the husband. She was given to be a helper, but proved a most grievous hinderer, even the instrument of his fall and ruin, on which the bond of subjection was confirmed, and tied faster on her (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.16">Gen. iii. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee,</hi> with less easiness, it may be, than before. It is therefore doubly enjoined: <hi type="italic">first in innocency,</hi> when was settled a subordination of nature, Adam being first formed and then Eve, and the woman being taken out of the man; <hi type="italic">and then upon the fall,</hi> the woman being first in the transgression, and seducing the man; here now began to be a subjection not so easy and comfortable, being a part of the penalty in her case; yet through Christ is this nevertheless a sanctified state. <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22-Eph.5.23">Eph. v. 22, 23</reference>, <hi type="italic">Wives submit yourselves unto you own husbands, as unto the Lord,</hi> as owning Christ's authority in them, whose image they bear; <hi type="italic">for the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body.</hi> God would have a resemblance of Christ's authority over the church held forth in the husband's over the wife. Christ is the head of the church, to protect and save it, to supply it with all good, and secure or deliver it from evil; and so the husband over the wife, to keep her from injuries, and to provide comfortably for her, according to his ability. Therefore, as the church is subject unto Christ, so let the <hi type="italic">wives be unto their own husbands, as is fit in the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col. iii. 18</reference>), as comports with the law of Christ, and is for his and the Father's glory. It is not then an absolute, or unlimited, nor a slavish subjection that is required; but a loving subordination, to prevent disorder or confusion, and to further all the ends of the relation. Thus, in reference to the husbands, wives must be instructed in their duties of love and subjection to them. <hi type="italic">And to love their children,</hi> not with a natural affection only, but a spiritual, a love springing from a holy sanctified heart and regulated by the word; not a fond foolish love, indulging them in evil, neglecting due reproof and correction where necessary, but a regular Christian love, showing itself in their pious education, forming their life and manners aright, taking care of their souls as well as of their bodies, of their spiritual welfare as well as of their temporal, of the former chiefly and in the first place. The reason is added: <hi type="italic">That the word of God may not be blasphemed.</hi> Failures in such relative duties would be greatly to the reproach of Christianity. "What are these the better for this their new religion?" would the infidels be ready to say. The word of God and the gospel of Christ are pure, excellent, and glorious, in themselves; and their excellency should be expressed and shown in the lives and conduct of their professors, especially in relative duties; failures here being disgrace. <reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Rom. ii. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles through you.</hi> "Judge what a God he is," would they be ready to say, "by these his servants; and what his word, and doctrine, and religion, are by these his followers." Thus would Christ <hi type="italic">be wounded in the house of his friends.</hi> Thus of the duties of the younger women. <div eID="gen32630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32631" type="x-p"/> 4. Here is the duty of young men. They are apt to be eager and hot, thoughtless and precipitant; therefore they must be earnestly called upon and exhorted to be considerate, not rash; advisable and submissive, not wilful and head-strong; humble and mild, not haughty and proud; for there are more young people ruined by pride than by any other sin. The young should be grave and solid in their deportment and manners, joining the seriousness of age with the liveliness and vigour of youth. This will make even those younger years to pass to good purpose, and yield matter of comfortable reflection when the evil days come; it will be preventive of much sin and sorrow, and lay the foundation for doing and enjoying much good. Such shall not <hi type="italic">mourn at the last,</hi> but have peace and comfort in death, and after it a glorious crown of life. <div eID="gen32631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32632" type="x-p"/> 5. With these instructions to Titus, respecting what he should teach others—the aged men and women, and the younger of both sexes (Titus himself probably at this time being a young man also), the apostle inserts some directions to himself. He could not expect so successfully to teach others, if he did not conduct himself well both in his conversation and preaching. (1.) Here is direction for his conversation: <hi type="italic">In all things showing thyself a pattern of good works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.7">v. 7</reference>. Without this, he would pull down with one hand what he built with the other. Observe, Preachers of good works must be patterns of them also; good doctrine and good life must go together. <hi type="italic">Thou that teachest another, teachest thou not thyself?</hi> A defect here is a great blemish and a great hindrance. <hi type="italic">In all things;</hi> some read, <hi type="italic">above all things,</hi> or <hi type="italic">above all men.</hi> Instructing others in the particulars of their duty is necessary, and, above all things, example, especially that of the teacher himself, is needful; hereby both light and influence are more likely to go together. "Let them see a lively image of those virtues and graces in thy life which must be in theirs. Example may both teach and impress the things taught; when they see purity and gravity, sobriety and all good life, in thee, they may be more easily won and brought thereto themselves; they may become pious and holy, sober and righteous, as thou art." Ministers must be examples to the flock, and the people followers of them, as they are of Christ. And here is direction, (2.) For his teaching and doctrine, as well as for his life: <hi type="italic">In doctrine showing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity, sound speech, that cannot be condemned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.7-Titus.2.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. They must make it appear that the design of their preaching is purely to advance the honour of God, the interest of Christ and his kingdom, and the welfare and happiness of souls; that this office was not entered into nor used with secular views, not from ambition nor covetousness, but a pure aim at the spiritual ends of its institution. In their preaching, therefore, the display of wit or parts, or of human learning or oratory, is not to be affected; but sound speech must be used, which cannot be <hi type="italic">condemned;</hi> scripture-language, as far as well may be, in expressing scripture-truths. This is sound speech, that cannot be condemned. We have more than once these duties of a minister set together. <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.16">1 Tim. iv. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">Take heed to thyself, and to thy doctrine:</hi> and, <reference osisRef="Titus.2.12">v. 12</reference>. of the same chapter, "<hi type="italic">Let no man despise thy youth, but be thou an example of believers in word</hi>—in thy speech, as a Christian, being grave, serious, and to the use of edifying; and in thy preaching, that it be the pure word of God, or what is agreeable to it and founded on it. Thus be an example <hi type="italic">in word:</hi> and <hi type="italic">in conversation,</hi> the life corresponding with the doctrine. In doing this <hi type="italic">thou shalt both save thyself and those that hear thee.</hi>" In <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10">2 Tim. iii. 10</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou hast fully known my doctrine and manner of life</hi> (says the same apostle), how agreeable these have been. And so must it be with others; their teaching must be agreeable to the word, and their life with their teaching. This is the true and good minister. <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.9-1Thess.2.10">1 Thess. ii. 9, 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Labouring night and day, we preached to you the gospel of God; and you are witnesses, and God also, how holily, and justly, and unblamably, we behaved ourselves among you.</hi> This must be looked to, as the next words show, which are, (3.) The reason both for the strictness of the minister's life and the gravity and soundness of his preaching: <hi type="italic">That he who is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you.</hi> Adversaries would be seeking occasion to reflect, and would do so could they find any thing amiss in doctrine or life; but, if both were right and good, such ministers might set calumny itself at defiance; they would have not evil thing to say justly, and so must be ashamed of their opposition. Observe, Faithful ministers will have enemies watching for their halting, such as will endeavour to find or pick holes in their teaching or behaviour; the more need therefore for them to look to themselves, that no just occasion be found against them. Opposition and calumny perhaps may not be escaped; men of corrupt minds will resist the truth, and often reproach the preachers and professors of it; but let them see that <hi type="italic">with well-doing they put to silence the ignorance of foolish men; that, when they speak evil of them as evil-doers; those may be ashamed who falsely accuse their good conversation in Christ.</hi> This is the direction to Titus himself, and so of the duties of free persons, male and female, old and young. Then follow, <div eID="gen32632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32633" type="x-p"/> 6. The directions respecting servants. Servants must not think that their mean and low state puts them beneath God's notice or the obligations of his laws—that, because they are servants of men, they are thereby discharged from serving God. No; servants must know and do their duty to their earthly masters, but with an eye to their heavenly one: and Titus must not only instruct and warn earthly masters of their duties, but servants also of theirs, both in his public preaching and private admonitions. Servants must attend the ordinances of God for their instruction and comfort, as well as the masters themselves. In this direction to Titus there are the duties themselves, to which he must exhort servants, and a weighty consideration wherewith he was to enforce them. <div eID="gen32633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32634" type="x-p"/> (1.) The duties themselves are these:— <div eID="gen32634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32635" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">To be obedient to their own masters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.9">v. 9</reference>. This is the prime duty, that by which they are characterized. <reference osisRef="Rom.6.16">Rom. vi. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">His servants you are whom you obey.</hi> There must be inward subjection and dutiful respect and reverence in the mind and thoughts. "<hi type="italic">If I be a master, where is my fear,</hi> the dutiful affection you show to me, together with the suitable outward significations and expressions of it, in doing what I command you?" This must be in servants; their will must be subject to their master's will, and their time and labour at their master's disposal and command. <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1 Pet. ii. 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward.</hi> The duty results from the will of God, and relation in which, by his providence, he has put such; not from the quality of the person. If he be a master, the duties of a servant are to be paid to him as such. Servants therefore are to be exhorted to be obedient to their own masters. And, <div eID="gen32635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32636" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">To please them well in all things,</hi> in all lawful things, and such as belong to them to command, or at least as are not contrary to the will of their great and superior Lord. We are not to understand it either of obeying or pleasing them absolutely, without any limitation; but always with a reserve of God's right, which may in no case be entrenched upon. If his command and the earthly master's come in competition, we are instructed to obey God rather than man; but then servants must be upon good grounds in this, that there is an inconsistency, else are they not held to be excused. And not only must the will of God be the measure of the servant's obedience, but the reason of it also. All must be done with a respect to him, in virtue of his authority, and for pleasing him primarily and chiefly, <reference osisRef="Col.3.22-Col.3.24">Col. iii. 22-24</reference>. In serving the earthly master according to Christ's will, he is served; and such shall be rewarded by him accordingly. But how are servants to please their masters in all things, and yet not be men-pleasers? <hi type="italic">Answer,</hi> Men-pleasers, in the faulty sense, are such as eye men alone, or chiefly, in what they do, leaving God out, or subordinating him to man; when the will of man shall carry it, though against God's will, or man's pleasure is more regarded than his,—when this can content them, that the earthly master is pleased, though God be displeased,—or when more care, or more satisfaction, is taken in man's being pleased than in God's, this is sinful man-pleasing, of which all must take heed. <reference osisRef="Eph.6.5-Eph.6.7">Eph. vi. 5-7</reference>, "<hi type="italic">Servants, be obedient to those that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, with singleness of your heart, as unto Christ. Not with eye-service, as men-pleasers</hi> (who look at nothing but the favour or displeasure of men, or at nothing so much as this), <hi type="italic">but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart; with good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men;</hi>" not to them chiefly, but to Christ, who requires, and who will reward, any good done, whether by bond or free. Observe therefore, Christian liberty comports well with civil servitude and subjection. Persons may serve men, and yet be the servants of Christ; these are not contrary, but subordinate, so far as serving men is according to Christ's will and for his sake. Christ came not to destroy or prejudice civil order and differences. "<hi type="italic">Art thou called, being a servant? Care not for it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">1 Cor. vii. 21</reference>. Let not this trouble thee, as if it were a condition unworthy of a Christian, or wherein the person so called is less pleasing unto God; <hi type="italic">for he that is called in the Lord, being a servant, is the Lord's freeman,</hi> not free from that service, but free in it; free spiritually, though not in a civil sense. <hi type="italic">Likewise also he that is called, being free, is Christ's servant;</hi> he is bound to him, though he be not under civil subjection to any; so that, <hi type="italic">bond or free, all are one in Christ.</hi>" Servants therefore should not regret nor be troubled at their condition, but be faithful and cheerful in the station wherein God hath set them, striving to please their masters in all things. Hard it may be under some churlish Nabals, but it must be aimed at as much as possible. <div eID="gen32636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32637" type="x-p"/> [3.] <hi type="italic">Not answering again;</hi> not contradicting them, nor disputing it with them; not giving them any disrespectful or provoking language. Job complained of his servants, that he <hi type="italic">called them, and they gave him no answer;</hi> that was faulty another way: <hi type="italic">Non respondere pro convitio est—Such silence is contempt:</hi> but here it is respect, rather to take a check or reproof with humble silence, not making any confident nor bold replies. When conscious of a fault, to palliate or stand in justification of it doubles it. Yet this not answering again excludes not turning away wrath with a soft answer, when season and circumstances admit. Good and wise masters will be ready to hear and do right; but answering unseasonably, or in an unseemly manner, or, where the case admits not excuse, to be pert or confident, shows a want of the humility and meekness which such relation requires. <div eID="gen32637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32638" type="x-p"/> [4.] <hi type="italic">Not purloining, but showing all good fidelity.</hi> This is another great essential of good servants, to be <hi type="italic">honest,</hi> never converting that to their own use which is their master's, nor wasting the goods they are entrusted with; that is, <hi type="italic">purloining.</hi> They must be just and true, and do for their masters as they would or should for themselves. <reference osisRef="Prov.28.24">Prov. xxviii. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">Whoso robbeth his father or his mother, and saith, It is no transgression, the same is the companion of a destroyer;</hi> he will be ready to join with him. Thus having such light thoughts of taking beyond what is right, though it be from a parent or master, is likely to harden conscience to go further; it is both wicked in itself, and it tends to more. Be it so that the master is hard and strait, scarcely making sufficient provision for servants; yet they must not be their own carvers, nor go about by theft to right themselves; they must bear their lot, committing their cause to God for righting and providing for them. I speak not of cases of extremity, for preserving life, the necessaries for which the servant has a right to. <hi type="italic">Not purloining, but showing all good fidelity;</hi> he must not only not steal nor waste, but must improve his master's goods, and promote his prosperity and thriving, to his utmost. He that increased not his master's talent is accused of unfaithfulness, though he had not embezzled nor lost it. Faithfulness in a servant lies in the ready, punctual, and thorough execution of his master's orders; keeping his secrets and counsels, despatching his affairs, and managing with frugality, and to as much just advantage for his master as he is able; looking well to his trusts, and preventing, as far as he can, all spoil, or loss, or damage. This is a way to bring a blessing upon himself, as the contrary often brings utter ruin. <hi type="italic">If you have not been faithful in that which is another man's, who shall give you that which is your own?</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.12">Luke xvi. 12</reference>. Thus of the duties themselves, to which servants are to be exhorted. Then, <div eID="gen32638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32639" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is the consideration with which Titus was to enforce them: <hi type="italic">That they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things;</hi> that is, that they may recommend the gospel and Christ's holy religion to the good opinion of those that are without, by their meek, humble, obedient, and faithful conduct in all things. Even servants, though they may think that such as they, in so low and inferior a condition, can do little to bring repute to Christianity, or adorn the doctrine of Christ, and set forth the excellences of his truth and ways, yet, if they be careful to do their duty, it will redound to the glory of God and the credit of religion. The unbelieving masters would think the better of that despised way, which was every where spoken against, when they found that those of their servants who were Christians were better than their other servants—more obedient and submissive, more just and faithful, and more diligent in their places. True religion is an honour to the professors of it; and they should see that they do not any dishonour to it, but adorn it rather in all that they are able. Our light must shine among men, so that they, seeing our good works, may glorify our Father who is in heaven. And thus of the apostle's directions to Titus, about the discharge of his office, in reference to several sorts of persons.
entries.2b56ca3c2bc2d738e757fc67a0b1642fc0392455: <div eID="gen32639" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Nature and Design of the Gospel; The Holy Tendency of the Gospel; Nature of Christ's Redemption. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32640" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, <hi type="super">12</hi> Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world; <hi type="super">13</hi> Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ; <hi type="super">14</hi> Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works. <div eID="gen32640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32641" type="x-p"/> Here we have the grounds or considerations upon which all the foregoing directions are urged, taken from the nature and design of the gospel, and the end of Christ's death. <div eID="gen32641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32642" type="x-p"/> I. From the nature and design of the gospel. Let young and old, men and women, masters and servants, and Titus himself, let all sorts do their respective duties, for this is the very aim and business of Christianity, to instruct, and help, and form persons, under all distinctions and relations, to a right frame and conduct. For this, <div eID="gen32642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32643" type="x-p"/> 1. They are put under the dispensation of <hi type="italic">the grace of God,</hi> so the gospel is called, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.2">Eph. iii. 2</reference>. It is grace in respect of the spring of it—the free favour and good-will of God, not any merit or desert in the creature; as manifesting and declaring this good-will in an eminent and signal manner; and as it is the means of conveying and working grace in the hearts of believers. Now grace is obliging and constraining to goodness: <hi type="italic">Let not sin reign, but yield yourselves unto God; for you are not under the law, but under grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.6.12-Rom.6.14">Rom. vi. 12-14</reference>. <hi type="italic">The love of Christ constrains us</hi> not to live to self, but to him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.14-2Cor.5.15">2 Cor. v. 14, 15</reference>); without this effect, grace is received in vain. <div eID="gen32643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32644" type="x-p"/> 2. This gospel grace <hi type="italic">brings salvation</hi> (reveals and offers it to sinners and ensures it to believers)—salvation from sin and wrath, from death and hell. Hence it is called <hi type="italic">the word of life;</hi> it brings to faith, and so to life, the life of holiness now and of happiness hereafter. The law is the ministration of death, but the gospel the ministration of life and peace. This therefore must be received as salvation (its rules minded, its commands obeyed), that the end of it may be obtained, <hi type="italic">the salvation of the soul.</hi> And more inexcusable will the neglecters of this grace of God bringing salvation now be, since, <div eID="gen32644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32645" type="x-p"/> 3. <hi type="italic">It hath appeared,</hi> or shone out more clearly and illustriously than ever before. The old dispensation was comparatively dark and shadowy; this is a clear and shining light; and, as it is now more bright, so more diffused and extensive also. For, <div eID="gen32645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32646" type="x-p"/> 4. It hath appeared <hi type="italic">to all men;</hi> not to the Jews only, as the glory of God appeared at mount Sinai to that particular people, and out of the view of all others; but gospel grace is open to all, and all are invited to come and partake of the benefit of it, Gentiles as well as Jews. The publication of it is free and general: <hi type="italic">Disciple all nations: Preach the gospel to every creature.</hi> The pale is broken down; there is no such enclosure now as formerly. <hi type="italic">The preaching of Jesus Christ, which was kept secret since the world began, now is made manifest, and by the scriptures of the prophets, according to the commandment of the everlasting God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.16.25-Rom.16.26">Rom. xvi. 25, 26</reference>. The doctrine of grace and salvation by the gospel is for all ranks and conditions of men (slaves and servants, as well as masters), therefore engaging and encouraging all to receive and believe it, and walk suitably to it, adorning it in all things. <div eID="gen32646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32647" type="x-p"/> 5. This gospel revelation is to <hi type="italic">teach,</hi> and not by way of information and instruction only, as a schoolmaster does his scholars, but by way of precept and command, as a sovereign who gives laws to his subjects. It directs what to shun and what to follow, what to avoid and what to do. The gospel is not for speculation only or chiefly, but for practice and right ordering of life; for it teaches us, <div eID="gen32647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32648" type="x-p"/> (1.) To abandon sin: <hi type="italic">Denying ungodliness and worldly lusts;</hi> to renounce and have no more to do with these, as we have had: <hi type="italic">Put off, concerning the former conversation, the old man which is corrupt;</hi> that is, the whole body of sins, here distributed into <hi type="italic">ungodliness</hi> and <hi type="italic">worldly lusts.</hi> "Put away ungodliness and irreligion, all unbelief, neglect or disesteem of the divine Being, not loving, nor fearing, nor trusting in him, nor obeying him as we should, neglecting his ordinances, slighting his worship, profaning his name or day. Thus deny ungodliness (hate and put it away); <hi type="italic">and worldly lusts,</hi> all corrupt and vicious desires and affections that prevail in worldly men, and carry out to worldly things <hi type="italic">the lust of the flesh also, and of the eye, and the pride of life,</hi> all sensuality and filthiness, covetous desires and ambition, seeking and valuing more the praise of men than of God; put away all these." An earthly sensual conversation suits not a heavenly calling. <hi type="italic">Those that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.</hi> They have done it by covenant-engagement and promise, and have initially and prevailingly done it in act; they are going on in the work, cleansing themselves more and more from all filthiness of flesh and spirit. Thus the gospel first unteaches that which is evil, to abandon sin; and then, <div eID="gen32648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32649" type="x-p"/> (2.) To make conscience of that which is good: <hi type="italic">To live soberly, righteously, and godly,</hi> &c. Religion is not made up of negatives only; there must be doing good as well as eschewing evil; in these conjunctly is sincerity proved and the gospel adorned. We should live soberly with respect to ourselves, in the due government of our appetites and passions, keeping the limits of moderation and temperance, avoiding all inordinate excesses; and righteously towards all men, rendering to all their due, and injuring none, but rather doing good to others, according to our ability and their need: this seems a part of justice and righteousness, for we are not born for ourselves alone, and therefore may not live to ourselves only. <hi type="italic">We are members one of another,</hi> and <hi type="italic">must seek every man another's wealth,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.24">1 Cor. x. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.25">xii. 25</reference>. The public, especially, which includes the interests of all, must have the regards of all. Selfishness is a sort of unrighteousness; it robs others of that share in us which is their due. How amiable then will a just and righteous conduct be! It secures and promotes all interests, not particular only, but general and public, and so contributes to the peace and happiness of the world. Live righteously therefore as well as soberly. And godly towards God, in the duties of his worship and service. Regards to him indeed should run through all. <hi type="italic">Whether you eat, or drink, or whatsoever you do, do all to the glory of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.31">1 Cor. x. 31</reference>. Personal and relative duties must be done in obedience to his commands, with due aim at pleasing and honouring him, from principles of holy love and fear of him. But there is an express and direct duty also that we owe to God, namely, belief and acknowledgment of his being and perfections, paying him internal and external worship and homage,—loving, fearing, and trusting in him,—depending on him, and devoting ourselves to him,—observing all those religious duties and ordinances that he has appointed,—praying to him, praising him, and meditating on his word and works. This is godliness, looking and coming to God, as our state now is, not immediately, but as he has manifested himself in Christ; so does the gospel direct and require. To go to God in any other way, namely, by saints or angels, is unsuitable, yea, contrary to the gospel rule and warrant. All communications from God to us are through his Son, and our returns must also be by him. God in Christ we must look at as the object of our hope and worship. Thus must we exercise ourselves to godliness, without which there can be no adorning of that gospel which is according to it, which teaches and requires such a deportment. A gospel conversation must needs be a godly conversation, expressing our love and fear and reverence of God, our hope and trust and confidence in him, as manifested in his Son. <hi type="italic">We are the circumcision</hi> (who have in truth what was signified by that sacrament) <hi type="italic">who worship God in the Spirit, and rejoice in Christ Jesus, and have no confidence in the flesh.</hi> See in how small a compass our duty is comprised; it is put into few words, <hi type="italic">denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, and living soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.</hi> The gospel teaches us not only how to believe and hope well, but also to live well, as becomes that faith and hope in this present world, and as expectants of another and better. There is the world that now is, and that which is to come; the present is the time and place of our trial, and the gospel teaches us to live well here, not, however, as our final state, but with an eye chiefly to a future: for it teaches us in all, <div eID="gen32649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32650" type="x-p"/> (3.) To look for the glories of another world, to which a sober, righteous, and godly life in this is preparative: <hi type="italic">Looking for that blessed hope, and the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.</hi> Hope, by a metonymy, is put for the thing hoped for, namely, heaven and the felicities thereof, called emphatically <hi type="italic">that hope,</hi> because it is the great thing we look and long and wait for; and a <hi type="italic">blessed hope,</hi> because, when attained, we shall be completely happy for ever. <hi type="italic">And the glorious appearing of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ.</hi> This denotes both the time of the accomplishing of our hope and the sureness and greatness of it: it will be at the second appearing of Christ, when he shall come <hi type="italic">in his own glory, and in his Father's, and of the holy angels,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.26">Luke ix. 26</reference>. His own glory which he had before the world was; and his Father's, being <hi type="italic">the express image of his person,</hi> and as God-man, his delegated ruler and Judge; and of the holy angels, as his ministers and glorious attendants. His first coming was in meanness, to satisfy justice and purchase happiness; his second will be in majesty, to bestow and instate his people in it. <hi type="italic">Christ was once offered to bear the sins of many; and unto those that look for him will he appear the second time, without sin, unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">Heb. ix. 28</reference>. <hi type="italic">The great God and our Saviour</hi> (or <hi type="italic">even our Saviour</hi>) <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ;</hi> for they are not two subjects, but one only, as appears by the single article, <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">tou megalou Theou kai Soteros,</hi></hi> not <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kai tou Soteros,</hi></hi> and so is <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">kai</hi></hi> rendered <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.24">1 Cor. xv. 24</reference>, <hi type="italic">When he shall have delivered up the kingdom to God, even the Father;</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">to Theo kai Patri.</hi></hi> Christ then is the <hi type="italic">great God,</hi> not figuratively, as magistrates and others are sometimes called gods, or as appearing and acting in the name of God, but properly and absolutely, <hi type="italic">the true God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.20">1 John v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">the mighty God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">Isa. ix. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.6">Phil. ii. 6</reference>. In his second coming he will reward his servants, and bring them to glory with him. Observe, [1.] There is a common and blessed hope for all true Christians in the other world. If in this life only they had hope in Christ, they were of all men the most miserable, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.19">1 Cor. xv. 19</reference>. By hope is meant the thing hoped for, namely, Christ himself, who is called <hi type="italic">our hope</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1 Tim. i. 1</reference>), and blessedness in and through him, even riches of glory (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Eph. i. 18</reference>), hence fitly termed here <hi type="italic">that blessed hope.</hi> [2.] The design of the gospel is to stir up all to a good life by this blessed hope. <hi type="italic">Gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and hope to the end for the grace that is to be brought unto you at the revelation of Jesus Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.13">1 Pet. i. 13</reference>. To the same purport here, <hi type="italic">Denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world, looking for the blessed hope;</hi> not as mercenaries, but as dutiful and thankful Christian. <hi type="italic">What manner of persons ought you to be in all holy conversation and godliness, looking for and hastening to the coming of the day of God!</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.11-2Pet.3.12">2 Pet. iii. 11, 12</reference>. Looking and hastening, that is, expecting and diligently preparing for it. [3.] At, and in, the glorious appearing of Christ will the blessed hope of Christians be attained; for their felicity will be this, <hi type="italic">To be where he is, and to behold his glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.24">John xvii. 24</reference>. The glory of the great God and our Saviour will then break out as the sun. Though in the exercise of his judiciary power he will appear as the Son of man, yet will he be mightily declared to be the Son of God too. The divinity, which on earth was much veiled, will shine out then as the sun in its strength. Hence the work and design of the gospel are to raise the heart to wait for this second appearing of Christ. <hi type="italic">We are begotten again to a lively hope of it</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.3">1 Pet. i. 3</reference>), turned to <hi type="italic">serve the living God, and wait for his Son from heaven,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.9-1Thess.1.10">1 Thess. i. 9, 10</reference>. Christians are marked by this, expecting their Master's coming (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.36">Luke xii. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">loving his appearance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 8</reference>. Let us then look to this hope; let our loins be girt, and our lights burning, and ourselves like those who wait for their Lord; the day or hour we know not, but <hi type="italic">he that shall come will come, and will not tarry,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.10.37">Heb. x. 37</reference>. [4.] The comfort and joy of Christians are that their Saviour is the great God, and will gloriously manifest himself at his second coming. Power and love, majesty and mercy, will then appear together in the highest lustre, to the terror and confusion of the wicked, but to the everlasting triumph and rejoicing of the godly. Were he not thus the great God, and not a mere creature, he could not be their Saviour, nor their hope. Thus of the considerations to enforce the directions of all sorts to their respective duties from the nature and design of the gospel. And herewith is connected another ground, namely, <div eID="gen32650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32651" type="x-p"/> II. From the end of Christ's death: <hi type="italic">Who gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify unto himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.2.14">v. 14</reference>. To bring us to holiness and happiness was the end of Christ's death, as well as the scope of his doctrine. Here we have, <div eID="gen32651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32652" type="x-p"/> 1. The purchaser of salvation—Jesus Christ, <hi type="italic">that great God and our Saviour,</hi> who saves not simply as God, much less as man alone; but as God-man, two natures in one person: man, that he might obey, and suffer, and die, for man, and be meet to deal with him and for him; and God, that he might support the manhood, and give worth and efficacy to his undertakings, and have due regard to the rights and honour of the deity, as well as the good of his creature, and bring about the latter to the glory of the former. Such a one became us; and this was, <div eID="gen32652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32653" type="x-p"/> 2. The price of our redemption: <hi type="italic">He gave himself.</hi> The Father gave him, but he gave himself too; and, in the freeness and voluntariness, as well as the greatness of the offering, lay the acceptableness and merit of it. <hi type="italic">Therefore doth my Father love me, because I lay down my life, that I might take it again. No man taketh it from me, but I lay it down of myself,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.10.17-John.10.18">John x. 17, 18</reference>. So <reference osisRef="John.17.19">John xvii. 19</reference>, "<hi type="italic">For their sakes I sanctify myself,</hi> or separate and devote myself to this work, to be both a priest and a sacrifice to God for the sins of men." The human nature was the offering, and the divine the altar, sanctifying the gift, and the whole the act of the person. <hi type="italic">He gave himself a ransom for all,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.6">1 Tim. ii. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">Once in the end of the world hath he appeared, to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself.</hi> He was the priest and sacrifice too. <hi type="italic">We are redeemed, not with silver and gold, but the precious blood of Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.18-1Pet.1.19">1 Pet. i. 18, 19</reference>), called <hi type="italic">the blood of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>), that is, of him who is God. <div eID="gen32653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32654" type="x-p"/> 3. The persons for whom: <hi type="italic">For us,</hi> us poor perishing sinners, gone off from God, and turned rebels against him. He gave himself <hi type="italic">for us,</hi> not only for our good, but in our stead. Messiah was cut off, not for himself, but for us. <hi type="italic">He suffered, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.18">1 Pet. iii. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">He was made sin for us</hi> (an offering and sacrifice for sin), <hi type="italic">that we might be made the righteousness of God in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2 Cor. v. 21</reference>. Wonderful condescension and grace! <hi type="italic">He loved us, and gave himself for us;</hi> what can we do less than love and give up ourselves to him? Especially considering, <div eID="gen32654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32655" type="x-p"/> 4. The ends of his giving himself for us, (1.) <hi type="italic">That he might redeem us from all iniquity.</hi> This is fitted to the first lesson, <hi type="italic">denying ungodliness and worldly lusts.</hi> Christ gave himself to redeem us from these, therefore put them away. To love and live in sin is to trample under foot redeeming blood, to despise and reject one of the greatest benefits of it, and to act counter to its design. But how could the short sufferings of Christ redeem us from all iniquity? <hi type="italic">Answer,</hi> Through the infinite dignity of his person. He who was God suffered, though not as God. The acts and properties of either nature are attributed to the person. God purchased his church <hi type="italic">with his own blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.28">Acts xx. 28</reference>. Could payment be made at once, no need of suffering for ever. A mere creature could not do this, from the finiteness of his nature; but God-man could. <hi type="italic">The great God and our Saviour gave himself for us:</hi> this accounts for it. <hi type="italic">By one offering he hath for ever perfected those that are sanctified,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.9.25-Heb.9.26">Heb. ix. 25, 26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.14">x. 14</reference>. He needed not to offer himself often, nor could he be holden of death, when he had once undergone it. Happy end and fruit of Christ's death, redemption from all iniquity! Christ died for this: and, (2.) <hi type="italic">To purify to himself a peculiar people.</hi> This enforces the second lesson: <hi type="italic">To live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.</hi> Christ died to purify as well as to pardon—to obtain grace, to heal the nature, as well as to free from guilt and condemnation. He gave himself for his church, <hi type="italic">to cleanse it.</hi> Thus does he make <hi type="italic">to himself a peculiar people,</hi> by purifying them. Thus are they distinguished from the world that lies in wickedness; they are born of God, and assimilated to him, bear his image, are holy as their heavenly Father is holy. Observe, Redemption from sin and sanctification of the nature go together, and both make a peculiar people unto God: freedom from guilt and condemnation, freedom from the power of lusts, and purification of soul by the Spirit. These are <hi type="italic">a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">a peculiar people.</hi> And, (3.) <hi type="italic">Zealous of good works.</hi> This peculiar people, as they are made so by grace purifying them, so must they be seen to be so by doing good, and a zeal therein. Observe, The gospel is not a doctrine of licentiousness, but of holiness and good life. We are redeemed from our vain conversation, to serve God <hi type="italic">in holiness and righteousness all the days of our life.</hi> Let us see then that we do good, and have zeal in it; only looking that zeal be guided by knowledge and spirited with love, directed to the glory of God, and always in some good thing. And thus of the motive to the duties directed, from the end of Christ's death.
entries.61fb1f4e7ffcf49fae1548d5b17b5f11dd9e0b8d: <div eID="gen32655" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortation to Various Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 66.)</title> <div sID="gen32656" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> These things speak, and exhort, and rebuke with all authority. Let no man despise thee. <div eID="gen32656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32657" type="x-p"/> The apostle closes the chapter (as he began it) with a summary direction to Titus upon the whole, in which we have the matter and manner of ministers' teaching, and a special instruction to Titus in reference to himself. <div eID="gen32657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32658" type="x-p"/> I. The matter of ministers' teaching: <hi type="italic">These thing,</hi> namely, those before mentioned: not Jewish fables and traditions, but the truths and duties of the gospel, of avoiding sin, and living soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world. Observe, Ministers in their preaching must keep close to the word of God. <hi type="italic">If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.11">1 Pet. iv. 11</reference>, and not the figments and inventions of his own brain. <div eID="gen32658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32659" type="x-p"/> II. The manner; by doctrine, and exhortation, and reproof with all authority. <reference osisRef="2Tim.3.16">2 Tim. iii. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable for doctrine, for reproof, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness;</hi> that is, to teach sound doctrine, to convince of sin and refute error, to reform the life, and to carry forward in what is just and good; <hi type="italic">that the man of God</hi> (the Christian or minister) <hi type="italic">may be perfect, thoroughly furnished to all good works</hi> that are to be practised by himself or to be taught to others. Here is what will furnish for all parts of his duty, and the right discharge of them. "<hi type="italic">These things speak,</hi> or teach; shun not to declare the whole counsel of God." The great and necessary truths and duties of the gospel, especially, these <hi type="italic">speak and exhort,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parakalei,</hi></hi> <hi type="italic">press with much earnestness.</hi> Ministers must not be cold and lifeless in delivering heavenly doctrine and precepts, as if they were indifferent things or of little concern; but they must urge them with earnestness suitable to their nature and importance; they must call upon persons to mind and heed, and not be <hi type="italic">hearers only, deceiving themselves; but doers of the word, that they may be blessed therein. And rebuke;</hi> convince and reprove such as contradict or gainsay, or neglect and do not receive the truth as they should, or retain it in unrighteousness—those who hear it not with such a believing and obedient mind and heart as they ought, but, instead of this (it may be) live in contrary practices, showing themselves stubborn and disobedient, and to every good work reprobate. <hi type="italic">Rebuke with all authority,</hi> as coming in the name of God, and armed with his threatenings and discipline, whoever make light of which will do it at their peril. Ministers are reprovers in the gate. <div eID="gen32659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32660" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a special instruction to Titus in reference to himself: "<hi type="italic">Let no man despise thee;</hi> that is, give no occasion to do so, nor suffer it without reproof, considering that <hi type="italic">he who despiseth despiseth not man, but God.</hi>" Or thus, "<hi type="italic">Speak and exhort these things,</hi> press them upon all, as they may respectively be concerned; with boldness and faithfulness reprove sin, and carefully look to thyself and thy own conduct, and then none will despise thee." The most effectual way for ministers to secure themselves from contempt is to keep close to the doctrine of Christ, and imitate his example—to preach and live well, and do their duty with prudence and courage; this will best preserve both their reputation and their comfort. <div eID="gen32660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32661" type="x-p"/> Perhaps too an admonition might be here intended to the people—that Titus, though young, and but a substitute of the apostle, yet should not be condemned by them, but considered and respected as a faithful minister of Christ, and encouraged and supported in his work and office. "<hi type="italic">Know those that labour among you, and are over you in the Lord, and admonish you; and esteem them</hi> <hi type="italic">very highly in love for their work's sake,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.12-1Thess.5.13">1 Thess. v. 12, 13</reference>. Mind their teaching, respect their persons, support them in their function, and, what in you lies, further their endeavours for the honour of God and the salvation of souls."  <chapter eID="Titus.2"/> <div eID="gen32661" type="x-p"/>

entries.9c8ee33a4a8732d2e12ac8b6269aa53e2923ffb7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18267"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Titus.2.1-Titus.2.15">Tit 2:1-15</reference>. Directions to Titus: How to Exhort Various Classes of Believers: The Grace of God in Christ Our Grand Incentive to Live Godly.</title> <div sID="gen37941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18267"/><hi type="bold">1. But ... thou--</hi>in contrast to the reprobate seducers stigmatized in <reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.16">15, 16</reference>. "He deals more in exhortations, because those intent on useless questions needed chiefly to be recalled to the study of a holy, moral life; for nothing so effectually allays men's wandering curiosity, as the being brought to recognize those duties in which they ought to exercise themselves" [Calvin].<div eID="gen37941" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37942" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">speak--</hi>without restraint: contrast <reference osisRef="Titus.1.11">Tit 1:11</reference>, "mouths ... stopped."<div eID="gen37942" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrine--</hi>"instruction" or "teaching." <div eID="gen37943" type="x-p"/>
entries.22c8b6ed6aa7672a72c81c17de1f4bcb9ec66764: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18268"/><div sID="gen37944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18268"/><hi type="bold">2. sober--</hi>Translated "vigilant," as sober men alone can be (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.2">1Ti 3:2</reference>). But "sober" here answers to "not given to wine," <reference osisRef="Titus.2.3">Tit 2:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">Tit 1:7</reference>.<div eID="gen37944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37945" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grave--</hi>"dignified"; behaving with reverent propriety.<div eID="gen37945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37946" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">temperate--</hi>"self-restrained"; "discreet" [Alford], (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.8">Tit 1:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.9">1Ti 2:9</reference>).<div eID="gen37946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37947" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">faith ... charity [love] ... patience--</hi>combined in <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>. "Faith, hope, charity" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.13">1Co 13:13</reference>). "Patience," Greek, "enduring perseverance," is the attendant on, and is supported by, "hope" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.7">1Co 13:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.1.3">1Th 1:3</reference>). It is the grace which especially becomes old men, being the fruit of ripened experience derived from trials overcome (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.3">Ro 5:3</reference>). <div eID="gen37947" type="x-p"/>
entries.b7f9de893f96809d1b82da02e3f07acfbb2dcd12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18269"/><div sID="gen37948" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18269"/><hi type="bold">3. behaviour--</hi>"deportment."<div eID="gen37948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as becometh holiness--</hi>"as becometh women consecrated to God" [Wahl]: being by our Christian calling priestesses unto God (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.3">Ep 5:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.10">1Ti 2:10</reference>). "Observant of sacred decorum" [Bengel].<div eID="gen37949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not false accusers--</hi>not slanderers: a besetting sin of some elderly women.<div eID="gen37950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37951" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given to much wine--</hi>the besetting sin of the Cretans (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.12">Tit 1:12</reference>). Literally, "enslaved to much wine." Addiction to wine is slavery (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.16">Ro 6:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.19">2Pe 2:19</reference>).<div eID="gen37951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teachers--</hi>in private: not in public (<reference osisRef="1Cor.14.34">1Co 14:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.2.11">1Ti 2:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.12">12</reference>); influencing for good the younger women by precept and example. <div eID="gen37952" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b56ce19ca64f7517e045ebc75b356b05fcaac12: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18270"/><div sID="gen37953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18270"/><hi type="bold">4. to be sober--</hi>Greek, "self-restrained," "discreet"; the same Greek as in <reference osisRef="Titus.2.2">Tit 2:2</reference>, "temperate." (But see on <reference osisRef="Titus.2.2">Tit 2:2</reference>; compare Note, <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.7">2Ti 1:7</reference>). Alford therefore translates, "That they school (admonish in their duty) the young women to be lovers of their husbands," &c. (the foundation of all domestic happiness). It was judicious that Titus, a young man, should admonish the young women, not directly, but through the older women. <div eID="gen37953" type="x-p"/>
entries.16d4171c50b7f1533b8dbc0081c301064498f99a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18271"/><div sID="gen37954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18271"/><hi type="bold">5. keepers at home--</hi>as "guardians of the house," as the Greek expresses. The oldest manuscripts read, "Workers at home": active in household duties (<reference osisRef="Prov.7.11">Pr 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">1Ti 5:13</reference>).<div eID="gen37954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37955" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>kind, beneficent (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.15">Mt 20:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.7">Ro 5:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1Pe 2:18</reference>). Not churlish and niggardly, but thrifty as housewives.<div eID="gen37955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">obedient--</hi>rather "submissive," as the Greek is translated; (see on <reference osisRef="Eph.5.21">Ep 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.24">Ep 5:24</reference>).<div eID="gen37956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their own--</hi>marking the duty of subjection which they owe them, as being their own husbands (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.22">Ep 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.18">Col 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen37957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37958" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">blasphemed--</hi>"evil spoken of." That no reproach may be cast on the Gospel, through the inconsistencies of its professors (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.8">Tit 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.24">Ro 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">6:1</reference>). "Unless we are virtuous, blasphemy will come through us to the faith" [Theophylact]. <div eID="gen37958" type="x-p"/>
entries.f701c035dae8a94f2235985ea7a8ae53218fdbbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18272"/><div sID="gen37959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18272"/><hi type="bold">6. Young--</hi>Greek, "The younger men."<div eID="gen37959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sober-minded--</hi>self-restrained [Alford]. "Nothing is so hard at this age as to overcome pleasures and follies" [Chrysostom]. <div eID="gen37960" type="x-p"/>
entries.89b86c053dac561aa7a7aafdaf0562c1f232b3e3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18273"/><div sID="gen37961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18273"/><hi type="bold">7. In--</hi>with respect to all things.<div eID="gen37961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37962" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thyself a pattern--</hi>though but a young man thyself. All teaching is useless unless the teacher's example confirm his word.<div eID="gen37962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37963" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in doctrine--</hi>in thy ministerial teaching (showing) uncorruptness, that is, untainted purity of motive on thy part (compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.3">2Co 11:3</reference>), so as to be "a pattern" to all. As "gravity," &c., refers to Titus himself, so "uncorruptness"; though, doubtless, uncorruptness of the doctrine will be sure to follow as a consequence of the Christian minister being of simple, uncorrupt integrity himself.<div eID="gen37963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37964" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gravity--</hi>dignified seriousness in setting forth the truth.<div eID="gen37964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37965" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sincerity--</hi>omitted in the oldest manuscripts. <div eID="gen37965" type="x-p"/>
entries.52cbc1377d69ac6c8cd59ea98114086aad476aaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18274"/><div sID="gen37966" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18274"/><hi type="bold">8. speech--</hi>discourse in public and private ministrations.<div eID="gen37966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37967" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that is of the contrary part--</hi>the adversary (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.9">Tit 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.25">2Ti 2:25</reference>), whether he be heathen or Jew.<div eID="gen37967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may be ashamed--</hi>put to confusion by the power of truth and innocence (compare <reference osisRef="Titus.2.5">Tit 2:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37969" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no evil thing--</hi>in our acts, or demeanor.<div eID="gen37969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37970" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of you--</hi>So one of the oldest manuscripts. Other very old manuscripts read, "of US," Christians. <div eID="gen37970" type="x-p"/>
entries.7183a3f70175994c7493162ec52154685b74785c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18275"/><div sID="gen37971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18275"/><hi type="bold">9. servants--</hi>"slaves."<div eID="gen37971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37972" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to please them well--</hi>"to give satisfaction" [Alford]. To be complaisant in everything; to have that zealous desire to gain the master's goodwill which will anticipate the master's wish and do even more than is required. The reason for the frequent recurrence of injunctions to slaves to subjection (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22">Col 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.1">1Ti 6:1</reference>, &c.; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.18">1Pe 2:18</reference>) was, that in no rank was there more danger of the doctrine of the spiritual equality and freedom of Christians being misunderstood than in that of slaves. It was natural for the slave who had become a Christian, to forget his place and put himself on a social level with his master. Hence the charge for each to abide in the sphere in which he was when converted (<reference osisRef="1Cor.7.20-1Cor.7.24">1Co 7:20-24</reference>).<div eID="gen37972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not answering again--</hi>in contradiction to the master: so the Greek, "not contradicting" [Wahl]. <div eID="gen37973" type="x-p"/>
entries.bcd8aad4447b6c02cd03b7d4dd07fa04f7bdad17: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18276"/><div sID="gen37974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18276"/><hi type="bold">10. Not purloining--</hi>Greek, "Not appropriating" what does not belong to one. It means "keeping back" dishonestly or deceitfully (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.2">Ac 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen37974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">showing--</hi>manifesting in acts.<div eID="gen37975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all--</hi>all possible.<div eID="gen37976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37977" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good--</hi>really good; not so in mere appearance (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.5">Ep 6:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.6.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.22-Col.3.24">Col 3:22-24</reference>). "The heathen do not judge of the Christian's doctrines from the doctrine, but from his actions and life" [Chrysostom]. Men will write, fight, and even die for their religion; but how few live for it! Translate, "That they may adorn the doctrine of our Saviour God," that is, God the Father, the originating author of salvation (compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.1">1Ti 1:1</reference>). God deigns to have His Gospel-doctrine adorned even by slaves, who are regarded by the world as no better than beasts of burden. "Though the service be rendered to an earthly master, the honor redounds to God, as the servant's goodwill flows from the fear of God" [Theophylact]. Even slaves, low as is their status, should not think the influence of their example a matter of no consequence to religion: how much more those in a high position. His love in being "our Saviour" is the strongest ground for our adorning His doctrine by our lives. This is the force of "For" in <reference osisRef="Titus.2.11">Tit 2:11</reference>. <div eID="gen37977" type="x-p"/>
entries.671ca396a4f56e260d076cb225d4ffb2bff92898: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18277"/><div sID="gen37978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18277"/><hi type="bold">11. the grace of God--</hi>God's gratuitous favor in the scheme of redemption.<div eID="gen37978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hath appeared--</hi>Greek, "hath been made to appear," or "shine forth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.2">Is 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.79">Lu 1:79</reference>). "hath been manifested" (<reference osisRef="Titus.3.4">Tit 3:4</reference>), after having been long hidden in the loving counsels of God (<reference osisRef="Col.1.26">Col 1:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.9">2Ti 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.10">10</reference>). The image is illustrated in <reference osisRef="Acts.27.20">Ac 27:20</reference>. The grace of God hath now been embodied in Jesus, the brightness of the Father's glory," manifested as the "Sun of righteousness," "the Word made flesh." The Gospel dispensation is hence termed "the day" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.5">1Th 5:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.8">8</reference>; there is a double "appearing," that of "grace" here, that of "glory," <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Rom.13.12">Ro 13:12</reference>). Connect it not as English Version, but, "The grace ... that bringeth salvation to all men hath appeared," or "been manifested" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.10">4:10</reference>).
